To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of a CT-MRI registration technique that is based on bony anatomy and that is independent of patient position is a valid method of registering CT and MRI images of the pelvis.
the accuracy of image registration is affected by the MRI position and the accuracy of the MRI scan, and that the target delineation and dose calculation are also affected by the MRI scan position.
the accuracy of the MRI-CT registration is affected by MRI scan position, which in turn affects the delineation of the prostate and the dose distribution.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: 1) the effect of MRI scan position in the radiotherapy process; 2) the effect of the MRI scan position on target delineation accuracy, and 3) the effect of target delineation accuracy on the dose distribution.
the development and evaluation of a new approach to the problem of automatic image registration.
the development of an image registration method for MRI-guided radiotherapy (RT) of the prostate, which is capable of correcting for the effects of patient setup errors and prostate motion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the influence of the MRI scan position in prostate cancer radiotherapy is not clinically significant.

MRI scans performed in the supine position with a full bladder and the prostate gland in its most anterior position should be used to define the clinical target volume and organs at risk in prostate cancer patients.
the use of MRI in prostate cancer treatment planning is beneficial in the majority of patients, but not for every patient and not in every case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the accuracy of MRI scan position has an influence on the accuracy of MRI-CT registration, target delineation, and the dose delivered to the prostate and organs at risk.
the accuracy of MRI scan position is a critical issue in the MRI-based treatment planning for prostatic radiotherapy and should be carefully evaluated before clinical application.
MRI scans acquired in different patient positions can be accurately registered to each other, and that this registration can be performed using a variety of methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of MRI for treatment planning is a valuable tool in radiotherapy for prostate cancer.
MRI positioning is important for prostate radiotherapy.

there is a strong correlation between the position of the patient in the MRI scan, as well as the position of the MRI in the CT scan, with the accuracy of image registration, target delineation, and dose calculation in the treatment planning of prostate cancer.
